screens.title: Branching, Merging, and Conflict Resolution in Git
screens.narratorSegment: Branching and merging are the tools that let teams work in parallel while keeping a stable main code line. In this chapter you will learn what a branch is, how to create and switch between branches, how merges can be fast-forward or create explicit merge commits, and how to recognize and resolve merge conflicts marked by Git. You will see concrete terminal commands to create and switch branches, an example Python file showing a conflict, and a step-by-step lab that walks you through producing and fixing a merge conflict. Understanding these skills matters because they keep your main branch stable, make collaboration predictable, and reduce the risk of regressions when multiple people change the same code. A practical example you will follow is adding logging on a feature branch while a teammate changes the same function on main, leading to a conflict you will resolve by combining both changes. By the end of the lesson you will be able to integrate changes safely, run simple checks after merges, and follow best practices so conflicts are easier to manage. Consider how branching can let you try ideas without fear: what feature would you isolate on its own branch next?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to create, manage, and delete branches; switch branches safely; merge changes into main with an understanding of fast-forward and three-way merges; recognize and resolve merge conflicts using conflict markers; and apply team-friendly branching strategies. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: the commands you use every day, the mental model for how history is combined, and the checklist you follow when conflicts appear. For example, you will practice creating a feature branch, adding a commit, then merging that branch back to main and observing whether Git performs a fast-forward or creates an explicit merge commit. You will also learn to open a conflicted file, interpret the conflict markers, and construct a combined solution before staging and committing. Finally, you'll learn why branching strategies like GitFlow or GitHub Flow give teams consistent rules for when to branch and when to merge. These objectives are chosen to make collaboration predictable and reduce costly regressions. As you work through the lab, keep a note of one branching rule your team could adopt to make merges smoother.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on practice and team practices you will adopt. You will be guided through a lab that starts from an initialized repository and walks through creating a feature branch, making changes, creating a conflicting change on main, and then performing a merge that produces a conflict to resolve. You will practice using the commands that create-and-switch in one step to avoid accidental states. Beyond commands, you'll learn branching strategy concepts like GitFlow and GitHub Flow and when to use a short-lived feature branch versus a long-lived branch. The goal is to make merges predictable: keep changes small, merge frequently, and pull main changes into long-running branches so integration happens often rather than all at once. Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Hands-on & Strategy
Practice lab overview
A 15-minute walkthrough will guide you from branch creation to conflict resolution using a small Python example. This strengthens muscle memory for the commands and the conflict workflow.
Lab steps
  1. Start with a clean repo and initial commit.
  2. Create a feature branch and modify a file.

Team tip
Pull or merge main into your feature branch regularly to reduce big conflicts later. Keep commits focused and test after merges.

screens.title: What is a Git branch?
screens.narratorSegment: A branch in Git is an independent line of development that points to a sequence of commits. Think of the main branch as the trunk of a tree and feature branches as limbs you grow to try new work. When you commit on a branch, those commits are recorded on that line alone until you merge them. This isolation is what makes branches powerful: you can implement a feature, fix a bug, or experiment without affecting the main or other branches. A common misconception is that branches copy the repository; they do not duplicate files in full. Instead, a branch is just a lightweight pointer to commits and the underlying storage is shared. Practically, you will create a branch for a feature, make multiple commits, and then merge when ready. For example, you might create feature/new-login, add logging and tests on that branch, and only merge when tests pass. Another misconception is that merging always changes history; sometimes a fast-forward merge simply moves a pointer, leaving commits unchanged. The takeaway is that branches let you organize work and reduce risk by deferring integration until the feature is ready. How could you use a short-lived branch to split a larger task into safe incremental steps?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A branch is a named pointer to a series of commits, allowing isolated development without copying the repository.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is a Git branch?
A branch names a line of commits so you can work independently without changing main until you merge.
  • Branches are pointers to commits, not full copies.
  • Use short-lived branches for focused work and merge frequently.
  • Branches support parallel development and safer CI/CD.
Example
git branch feature/new-login # creates branch
git switch feature/new-login # switches to it
Key Takeaway

Branches isolate work using lightweight pointers so many developers can work concurrently without corrupting main.

Metaphor
Visualize the repository as a tree. Main is the trunk; each feature branch is a limb that grows new commits until it is merged back.
Common Misconception
Branches duplicate files. In reality they are pointers reusing the same objects, so branching is cheap and fast.
Try this
Create a short-lived branch for a one-step change and merge it back quickly to practice the workflow.

screens.title: Branch commands you need
screens.narratorSegment: Working with branches requires a small, reliable set of commands you will use every day. To inspect branches locally use the command that lists branches. To create a branch without switching, use the create command with the branch name. If you want to create and switch in one step, use the modern create-and-switch command which both makes the branch and places you on it. To just switch between existing branches, use the switching command which is a safer alternative to earlier checkout behavior. Finally, delete a branch when it is no longer needed. A common mistake is creating a branch but forgetting to switch to it, so new commits land on the wrong branch; the create-and-switch form avoids this. Practice sequence: list, create-and-switch, commit work, switch back to main, and merge. For example, create a feature branch for logging, make commits there, then switch to main before merging back. Remember that deleting a branch locally after merge keeps history while removing the pointer. The skill is not just memorizing commands but following a consistent workflow that prevents commits from ending up on the wrong branch. After you try these commands, ask yourself which form reduces accidental mistakes for you.

keyIdea.title: Common commands
keyIdea.text: Use list, create, switch, and delete operations to manage branch lifecycle and prevent accidental commits on the wrong branch.

content.html:
Process Flow
Branch commands you need
A short flow of operations that keeps your branch work predictable and safe.
1
Inspect branches
git branch
2
Create and switch
git switch -c feature/add-logging
3
Switch without creating
git switch main
4
Delete local branch
git branch -d feature/old
Example workflow
List branches, create-and-switch to feature/add-logging, make commits, switch back to main, merge the feature branch when ready.
Common mistake
Forgetting to switch to a newly created branch. Use create-and-switch to avoid it.
Key Takeaway

Prefer the create-and-switch command to reduce accidental commits on main and keep your branch lifecycle simple.

screens.title: Fast-forward vs Three-way merge
screens.narratorSegment: When merging a feature branch into a target branch, Git chooses one of two common behaviors: fast-forward or three-way merge. A fast-forward merge happens when the target branch has not moved since the feature branch was created. In that case Git simply moves the target branch pointer forward to the feature commit and no new merge commit is created. This keeps history linear and is easy to read. In contrast, a three-way merge is used when both branches have new commits since they diverged. Git computes a new merge commit with two parents that explicitly records the integration of both lines of work. A three-way merge preserves the branching history and is useful when you want a record that work from two branches was brought together. A frequent misconception is that one merge form is always better; in practice, each has trade-offs. Fast-forward produces a tidy linear history but removes the explicit boundary between the feature and main. Three-way merges create a documented integration point. When collaborating in teams, pick a convention: some teams prefer always creating a merge commit to mark feature integration, while others rebase or fast-forward for a linear log. Practice both forms so you can explain why your team prefers one approach. Which history style helps you trace feature work later?

keyIdea.title: Merge types
keyIdea.text: Fast-forward moves a pointer when no divergence exists; three-way creates a merge commit when histories have diverged.

content.html:
Comparison
Fast-forward vs Three-way merge
Two distinct behaviors for integrating branches with different historical shapes.
Fast-forward
Occurs when target branch hasn't advanced. Git moves the pointer forward; no merge commit is created. History remains linear.
Three-way merge
Used when both branches have new commits. Git creates a new merge commit with two parents, explicitly recording integration.
Diagram (conceptual)
Imagine the feature branch being ahead with no changes on main — fast-forward. If main also moved, you get a merge commit that ties both lines together.
Team decision
Agree with your team whether to allow fast-forwards, always create merge commits, or rebase before merging to shape history consistently.
Key Takeaway

Both merge types are valid; choose the one that gives your team the right balance between a clear audit trail and linear history.

screens.title: What causes a merge conflict?
screens.narratorSegment: A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically reconcile changes to the same lines in the same files across two branches. This typically happens when two developers edit the same function or remove and modify the same line in different ways. Git signals a conflict by stopping the merge and inserting conflict markers into the affected files. These markers show the current branch content, a separator, and the incoming branch content. A common example is when you add logging on a feature branch while someone on main changes the same return statement; Git cannot decide which version preserves intent. It's important to know that conflicts are not errors in Git, they are prompts to choose how to combine work intentionally. A frequent misconception is that conflicts indicate a broken repository; actually they are a normal part of collaborative workflows and must be handled deliberately. The standard resolution workflow is: open the conflicted file, edit to combine or choose the correct code, remove the markers, stage the file, and commit the merge. Run your tests after resolution because resolving markers by hand can introduce logic errors. Finally, reduce conflict likelihood by communicating, making smaller changes, and merging main into long-lived branches frequently.

keyIdea.title: Merge conflict
keyIdea.text: Conflicts occur when the same lines change differently on branches; they require manual resolution and careful testing after combining changes.

content.html:
Definition
What causes a merge conflict?
Conflicts happen when Git can't automatically decide which change to keep for the same lines in a file.
  • Same lines changed differently across branches triggers a conflict.
  • Git marks conflicts and pauses the merge until you resolve them.
  • After resolution, stage the files and commit to finish the merge.
Conflict markers example
 <<<<<< HEAD
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name.upper()}!"
=======
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

def greet(name):
    logging.info(f"Greeting {name}")
    return f"Hello, {name}!"
>>>>>> feature/add-logging
Resolution checklist
  1. Edit file to combine changes and remove markers.
  2. Stage resolved files with the add command.
  3. Commit to complete the merge and run tests.
Common mistake
Forgetting to stage resolved files before committing leaves the merge incomplete. Always run status to confirm.
Key Takeaway

Conflicts are normal. Treat them as prompts to make intentional decisions about combined code and verify with tests.

screens.title: Conflict example in app.py
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete conflict using a small Python file called app dot P Y file. On the feature branch we add logging and keep the original greeting. On main someone removed logging and changed the greeting to uppercase. When you attempt to merge the feature branch into main, Git inserts conflict markers showing the two versions. Your task is to edit the file to combine both changes — keep the logging calls and apply the uppercase transform — then remove the conflict markers. After editing, stage the file and commit the merge. A common misconception is that you must choose one version entirely; instead combine thoughtfully and preserve behavior the team expects. The example resolution maintains logging and returns an uppercase greeting, which is a sensible merge of both intentions. After staging and committing, run your application or tests to ensure behavior matches expectations. This example shows the full sequence from conflict to resolution and underscores why manual review and testing are essential after resolving conflicts. Conflict example in app.py means combine conflicting edits intentionally, stage the resolved file, and commit. then run tests to confirm behavior.. In practical terms, a concrete conflict and its manual resolution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Example resolution
keyIdea.text: Combine conflicting edits intentionally, stage the resolved file, and commit. Then run tests to confirm behavior.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Conflict example in app.py
A hands-on conflict produced by different edits on main and a feature branch; resolve by combining intent.
Conflicted file content (as shown by Git)
 <<<<<< HEAD
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name.upper()}!"
=======
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format='%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')

def greet(name):
    logging.info(f"Greeting {name}")
    return f"Hello, {name}!"
>>>>>> feature/add-logging
Resolved file keeps logging and applies uppercase to the returned greeting so both intentions are preserved.
Resolved version (example)
# app.py
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format='%(asctime)s - %(levelname)s - %(message)s')

def greet(name):
    logging.info(f"Greeting {name}")
    return f"Hello, {name.upper()}!"

if __name__ == '__main__':
    user_name = "DevOps Learner"
    print(greet(user_name))
Steps to resolve
  1. Edit file to combine both changes and remove markers.
  2. Stage with git add and then commit the merge.
  3. Run tests or run the application to verify behavior.
Common Mistake
Committing without staging resolved files will leave the merge incomplete. Always check git status before committing.
Key Takeaway

Resolve conflicts by combining code intentions, stage the resolved files, and test the result thoroughly.

screens.title: Merge resolution workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Resolving a merge requires a clear sequence of steps to avoid leaving the repository in an inconsistent state. Start by attempting the merge; if Git reports a conflict, run the status command to see which files are unmerged. Open each conflicted file and locate the conflict markers. Edit the file to choose or combine changes, and remove the markers so the file is syntactically correct. After editing, stage each resolved file. A common pitfall is forgetting to stage resolved files. Once all conflicts are staged, create the merge commit with an explanatory message. Finally, run your test suite or a quick manual check to confirm that behavior matches expectations. If you use a graphical merge tool, it still follows the same flow: manual decision, stage, and commit. When working with remotes, push the result after committing and communicate to collaborators about the resolution. This workflow reduces surprises and preserves a clear record of decisions made during the merge. Reflect on a time when a missing test revealed a bad merge — what step would have caught it earlier? Merge resolution workflow means identify conflicted files, edit to combine or choose changes, stage them, commit the merge, and verify with tests.. In practical terms, from conflict detection to verified merge commit. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Resolution workflow
keyIdea.text: Identify conflicted files, edit to combine or choose changes, stage them, commit the merge, and verify with tests.

content.html:
Process Flow
Merge resolution workflow
A concrete checklist to finish merges safely when conflicts appear.
1. Try the merge and observe Git output
Git will stop and mark files when automatic merge fails.
2. Run git status
Find files listed as unmerged so you know where to edit.
3. Edit conflicted files and remove markers
Combine both intentions when possible and keep the code functional.
4. Stage and commit
git add each file, then commit with a message explaining the resolution.
Tip
Use git status often and run tests before and after merges to catch regressions early.
Pro tip
If a conflict is large, consider discussing it with the other author before choosing a resolution to preserve intent.
Key Takeaway

Follow the checklist to resolve conflicts reliably: identify, edit, stage, commit, and verify.

Best Practices
Branching strategies for teams
Rules help teams reduce integration friction and make responsibilities clear.
GitFlow
Structured with long-lived develop, release, and hotfix branches. Good for formal releases but needs coordination.
GitHub Flow
Short-lived branches merged into main quickly with CI. Works well for continuous deployment and smaller teams.
Cross-cutting rules
  • Keep branches small and merge frequently.
  • Pull or merge main into features to reduce conflicts.
  • Require tests and code review before merging.
Protection
Protect main with branch protection rules and require passing CI to avoid accidental regressions.
Key Takeaway

Agree on a branching strategy and enforce it with automated checks to make merges predictable and safer.

screens.title: Mistakes that make conflicts worse
screens.narratorSegment: Certain habits increase the likelihood or severity of merge conflicts. Making large, unrelated changes on a single branch, delaying merges for long periods, and failing to pull main changes into your feature branch are common culprits. Another frequent mistake is editing binary files or formatted data in conflicting ways that are hard to merge. Forgetting to stage resolved files before committing leaves the repository in a still-conflicted state, which can confuse collaborators. Also avoid resolving conflicts by deleting the other person's code without discussion; that can silently remove intent or important fixes. The antidote is small, focused commits, frequent integration with main, and clear communication when overlapping work is planned. Use branch naming conventions to signal intent and keep pull requests small so reviewers can reason about changes. Finally, always run tests and a quick manual check after resolving conflicts. If you find yourself repeatedly resolving the same kinds of conflicts, bring that pattern to your team's retrospective and adjust the workflow or boundaries between areas of ownership. Mistakes that make conflicts worse means make small focused changes, merge often, stage resolved files, and communicate with teammates to minimize painful conflicts.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Common Mistakes
Mistakes that make conflicts worse
Avoid habits that amplify merge pain and make conflict resolution harder than it needs to be.
  • Large, unrelated changes grouped into one branch make merges risky.
  • Long-lived branches that rarely integrate with main create bigger conflicts.
  • Forgetting to stage resolved files before committing leaves the merge incomplete.
Practical advice
Break work into smaller PRs, merge main into features often, and keep an automated test gate before merges.
Pro Tip

If a conflict is confusing, pause and talk to the other author to preserve intent rather than guessing.

Key Takeaway

Smaller changes, frequent integration, and good communication make conflicts manageable and faster to resolve.

screens.title: Applying these skills in CI/CD
screens.narratorSegment: Branching and merge workflows play a central role in continuous integration and continuous delivery pipelines. In a CI/CD setup, each branch or pull request typically triggers automated builds and tests. That means when you merge a feature branch, any unresolved conflicts or failing tests are caught before deployment. Using short-lived branches that get tested frequently reduces the chance of broken builds on main. Teams often protect main by requiring all checks to pass before allowing a merge. A practical point is to run unit tests and linters on both feature branches and the merge result. This helps catch integration issues that only appear when two lines of work combine. Another useful pattern is to merge main into a feature branch and run tests locally or in CI before creating a pull request; this surfaces conflicts earlier. Remember that resolving conflicts locally without running tests can still introduce regressions. The best practice is to resolve, stage, commit, and then let CI validate the merged state before pushing to production. Ask how your team could add one automated check that would have prevented a recent bug.

Branching and merging are the tools that let teams work in parallel while keeping a stable main code line. In this chapter you will learn what a branch is, how to create and switch between branches, how merges can be fast-forward or create explicit merge commits, and how to recognize and resolve merge conflicts marked by Git. You will see concrete terminal commands to create and switch branches, an example Python file showing a conflict, and a step-by-step lab that walks you through producing and fixing a merge conflict. Understanding these skills matters because they keep your main branch stable, make collaboration predictable, and reduce the risk of regressions when multiple people change the same code. A practical example you will follow is adding logging on a feature branch while a teammate changes the same function on main, leading to a conflict you will resolve by combining both changes. By the end of the lesson you will be able to integrate changes safely, run simple checks after merges, and follow best practices so conflicts are easier to manage. Consider how branching can let you try ideas without fear: what feature would you isolate on its own branch next?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to create, manage, and delete branches; switch branches safely; merge changes into main with an understanding of fast-forward and three-way merges; recognize and resolve merge conflicts using conflict markers; and apply team-friendly branching strategies. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: the commands you use every day, the mental model for how history is combined, and the checklist you follow when conflicts appear. For example, you will practice creating a feature branch, adding a commit, then merging that branch back to main and observing whether Git performs a fast-forward or creates an explicit merge commit. You will also learn to open a conflicted file, interpret the conflict markers, and construct a combined solution before staging and committing. Finally, you'll learn why branching strategies like GitFlow or GitHub Flow give teams consistent rules for when to branch and when to merge. These objectives are chosen to make collaboration predictable and reduce costly regressions. As you work through the lab, keep a note of one branching rule your team could adopt to make merges smoother.

This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on practice and team practices you will adopt. You will be guided through a lab that starts from an initialized repository and walks through creating a feature branch, making changes, creating a conflicting change on main, and then performing a merge that produces a conflict to resolve. You will practice using the commands that create-and-switch in one step to avoid accidental states. Beyond commands, you'll learn branching strategy concepts like GitFlow and GitHub Flow and when to use a short-lived feature branch versus a long-lived branch. The goal is to make merges predictable: keep changes small, merge frequently, and pull main changes into long-running branches so integration happens often rather than all at once. A concrete practice is to fetch or merge main into your feature daily when others are active, which reduces the chance of large conflicts. After the lab, you should be able to walk through a conflict, edit the markers to combine code, stage the resolved file, and finalize the merge with a commit message that documents the resolution.

A branch in Git is an independent line of development that points to a sequence of commits. Think of the main branch as the trunk of a tree and feature branches as limbs you grow to try new work. When you commit on a branch, those commits are recorded on that line alone until you merge them. This isolation is what makes branches powerful: you can implement a feature, fix a bug, or experiment without affecting the main or other branches. A common misconception is that branches copy the repository; they do not duplicate files in full. Instead, a branch is just a lightweight pointer to commits and the underlying storage is shared. Practically, you will create a branch for a feature, make multiple commits, and then merge when ready. For example, you might create feature/new-login, add logging and tests on that branch, and only merge when tests pass. Another misconception is that merging always changes history; sometimes a fast-forward merge simply moves a pointer, leaving commits unchanged. The takeaway is that branches let you organize work and reduce risk by deferring integration until the feature is ready. How could you use a short-lived branch to split a larger task into safe incremental steps?

Working with branches requires a small, reliable set of commands you will use every day. To inspect branches locally use the command that lists branches. To create a branch without switching, use the create command with the branch name. If you want to create and switch in one step, use the modern create-and-switch command which both makes the branch and places you on it. To just switch between existing branches, use the switching command which is a safer alternative to earlier checkout behavior. Finally, delete a branch when it is no longer needed. A common mistake is creating a branch but forgetting to switch to it, so new commits land on the wrong branch; the create-and-switch form avoids this. Practice sequence: list, create-and-switch, commit work, switch back to main, and merge. For example, create a feature branch for logging, make commits there, then switch to main before merging back. Remember that deleting a branch locally after merge keeps history while removing the pointer. The skill is not just memorizing commands but following a consistent workflow that prevents commits from ending up on the wrong branch. After you try these commands, ask yourself which form reduces accidental mistakes for you.

When merging a feature branch into a target branch, Git chooses one of two common behaviors: fast-forward or three-way merge. A fast-forward merge happens when the target branch has not moved since the feature branch was created. In that case Git simply moves the target branch pointer forward to the feature commit and no new merge commit is created. This keeps history linear and is easy to read. In contrast, a three-way merge is used when both branches have new commits since they diverged. Git computes a new merge commit with two parents that explicitly records the integration of both lines of work. A three-way merge preserves the branching history and is useful when you want a record that work from two branches was brought together. A frequent misconception is that one merge form is always better; in practice, each has trade-offs. A merge conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically reconcile changes to the same lines in the same files across two branches. This typically happens when two developers edit the same function or remove and modify the same line in different ways. Finally, reduce conflict likelihood by communicating, making smaller changes, and merging main into long-lived branches frequently.
